Chapman
CHAP-man
noun
From Old English cēapman, a trader or dealer, from cēap (trade, bargain, price—the root also of cheap and chaffer) + man: a man of trade, a merchant or peddler. It renders the Hebrew participle of trafficking men who traded with Solomon.

Biblical Definition

A chapman is a trader, a dealer, a travelling merchant—a man of cheap in its old sense of trade and bargain. The word appears but once in the KJV, in the account of Solomon’s golden splendour: the yearly weight of gold that came to him was besides that which chapmen and merchants brought (2Ch 9:14), the traders and dealers whose caravans, with the kings of Arabia and the governors of the country, poured gold and silver into Jerusalem. The chapmen figure the reach of Solomon’s peace and wisdom, when the nations came bringing tribute to the son of David on his throne—a shadow, dim but real, of a greater Son of David to whom the kings shall bring presents and all nations serve. Scripture knows the merchant in many places: the virtuous woman maketh fine linen, and selleth it; and delivereth girdles unto the merchant (Pro 31:24), honest trade as a fruit of diligence; and the kingdom of heaven is likened to a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls, who sold all he had to buy the one of great price (Mat 13:45). Yet the trader can also stand for the world under judgment: the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over fallen Babylon (Rev 18:11), when their traffic in her luxuries comes to nothing in a day. The chapman thus teaches a double lesson: lawful commerce is a good gift, and the wealth of nations may serve the throne of the true Solomon; but the merchant who lays up treasure in Babylon, and not in the pearl of great price, shall mourn when her market fails.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CHAPMAN as a cheapener; one who offers as a purchaser; a market-man; a buyer or seller; a trader.

expand to see more

CHAPMAN, n. — A cheapener; one that offers as a purchaser; a buyer; a trader. Beside that which chapmen and merchants brought (2Ch 9:14).

CHAPMAN, n. — A market-man; a dealer in goods; one who buys and sells; a peddler or itinerant trader.

CHAPMAN, n. — One who chaffers or bargains; from the old sense of cheap, trade or price.

CHAP, v. — To cheapen; to bargain; to chaffer—the root verb, now obsolete, behind the trader’s name.

CHAPMEN, n. plur. — Traders; dealers; those who traffic in merchandise, as the chapmen who brought gold to Solomon.

Key Scripture

2Ch 9:14 — "Beside that which chapmen and merchants brought. And all the kings of Arabia and governors of the country brought gold and silver to Solomon."

Pro 31:24 — "She maketh fine linen, and selleth it; and delivereth girdles unto the merchant."

Mat 13:45 — "Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls:"

Rev 18:11 — "And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more:"

Modern Corruption

A KJV hapax for a trader, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the double lesson of commerce—lawful trade as a good gift and a tribute to the true Solomon, yet a snare to the merchant who lays up his treasure in Babylon.

expand to see more

The chapman rebukes the age’s making of trade into a god. Commerce is a good gift: the chapmen brought their gold to Solomon, the virtuous woman sold her linen and girdles with honest diligence, and the merchant seeking goodly pearls became the Lord’s own figure for the soul that will part with all for the kingdom. But the same trading heart, unmoored from God, becomes the merchant of Babylon, weeping over a fallen market because his treasure was all in the merchandise that no man buys any more. The temptation is not to trade but to trust the trade—to reckon a man’s life by the abundance of his traffic, to buy and sell and get gain while laying up nothing toward God. The word sets the honest chapman beside the Babylonish merchant and asks where a man’s treasure truly lies.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that all lawful commerce is to serve the throne of the true Solomon and the seeking of the pearl of great price. The chapmen who brought gold to Solomon foreshadow the nations bringing their glory to Christ, to whom the kings shall bring presents and every knee shall bow. Let the believer trade honestly, sell his linen and deliver his girdles, and prosper as God gives—but let him be above all the merchant man who, finding one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had and bought it. The chapman who gains the whole world and loses that pearl has made the worst bargain of all; the wise trader buys the field for the treasure hid therein.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English cēapman (trader), from cēap (trade, bargain—root of cheap) + man — a merchant or dealer; the KJV hapax of the chapmen who brought gold to Solomon.

expand to see more

Old English cēap — trade, bargain, price; the root also of cheap and chaffer, naming the act of buying and selling.

Old English cēapman — a man of trade, merchant, or dealer; the compound behind the KJV word.

Hebrew tār / the participle of trafficking men (2Ch 9:14) — the traders and dealers who brought gold to Solomon.

Hebrew rākal / sōchēr (H5503) — to go about as a trader, to traffic; the common word for merchant (Pro 31:24; Eze 27).

English cheap, chaffer, chapbook — the surviving kin, all keeping the old sense of trade and bargaining.

Usage

"Beside that which chapmen and merchants brought—the traders whose caravans poured gold into Solomon’s Jerusalem, a shadow of the nations bringing tribute to the true Son of David."

"The virtuous woman delivereth girdles unto the merchant: honest trade as a fruit of diligence, and a good gift of God rightly used."

"The merchant of Babylon weeps when his market fails; the merchant man seeking goodly pearls sold all he had for the one of great price—the chapman must choose where his treasure lies."
